title: Score the retrieval, then the answer
brief: A RAG answer is wrong. The labels you hold, the number of chunks an answer needs and the completeness of your judgments are all unspecified. Pick the metrics that say which half broke before you touch the prompt.

blocks.caption: Rank metrics for retrieval, from the Manning information retrieval text and common practice [[r25]]
head: Metric
Question it answers
Needs
Blind spot
rows: Precision at k
Of the top k, how many are relevant?
Binary labels
Least stable standard measure. A perfect system scores at most 0.4 at k = 20 when only 8 chunks are relevant.
Recall at k
How many of all relevant chunks reached the top k?
A complete list of relevant chunks per query
Ignores order inside the top k. Incomplete labels distort it.
Hit rate at k
Did at least one relevant chunk reach the top k?
One known relevant chunk per query
Says nothing about the rest or the order. A conventional definition, not a named Foundry evaluator.
MRR
How early did the first correct chunk appear?
One known correct chunk
Ignores everything ranked after the first hit.
MAP
Average precision at each relevant rank, averaged over queries
Complete binary labels
Good discrimination and stability, but binary relevance only.
nDCG at k
Are highly relevant chunks ranked above partly relevant ones?
Graded labels
Two gain formulas exist, so scores differ across tools.

blocks.title: nDCG at k with two gain choices
blocks.expr:
DCG@k = sum over i = 1..k of gain(rel_i) / log2(i + 1)
nDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k

vars.v: 2^rel_i - 1, common in industry and stresses highly relevant chunks
DCG@k of the ideal ordering, so a perfect ranking scores 1

blocks.example: Ranked relevance 3, 2, 0, 1. Linear gain gives **0.985**. Exponential gain gives **0.993**. Same ranking, different library, different number [[r46]]. MRR for first-relevant ranks 1, 3, none, 2 is (1 + 0.333 + 0 + 0.5) / 4 = **0.458**.

blocks.title: Pick the retrieval metric
blocks.prompt: Flip what you know about labels, evidence needs and judgment coverage. The ranking and the reasons update.

options.name: MRR
options.summary: Rank of the first correct chunk.

options.name: Hit rate at k
options.summary: Share of queries with a relevant chunk in the top k.

options.name: Recall at k
options.summary: Share of all relevant chunks found in the top k.

options.name: nDCG at k
options.summary: Graded relevance with a rank discount.

options.name: Judged context metrics
options.summary: RAGAS context precision and recall, or the Foundry Retrieval evaluator.

qrels.why: It needs a known correct chunk per query, which qrels supply.

none.why: Without a known correct chunk there is nothing to rank against.

one.why: It rewards the first correct chunk, which is all the answer needs.

many.why: It ignores every chunk after the first hit.

complete.why: The first judged-relevant rank is trustworthy.

holes.why: An unjudged but relevant chunk ranked first counts as a miss.

qrels.why: One known relevant chunk per query is enough to score it.

none.why: It still needs at least one known relevant chunk.

one.why: The question is whether a good chunk made it into the prompt.

many.why: It says nothing about the other chunks the answer needs.

holes.why: Less sensitive, since only one judged hit is required.

qrels.why: Counts judged relevant chunks that were found.

none.why: The denominator is the list of relevant chunks, which you do not have.

one.why: Overkill when a single chunk answers the question.

many.why: It measures whether every needed chunk arrived.

holes.why: Unjudged relevant chunks are invisible, so the denominator is a partial list.

qrels.why: Needs graded labels, which cost more than binary ones.

none.why: There are no grades to discount.

one.why: Fine, but MRR gives the same signal with fewer labels.

many.why: It rewards ranking highly relevant chunks above partial ones.

complete.why: Grades cover the ranking, so the discount is meaningful.

holes.why: Holes drag the score down. Check holes_ratio first.

qrels.why: Works, but rank metrics are cheaper and deterministic.

none.why: A judge reads the retrieved chunks directly, so no qrels are needed.

many.why: Context recall checks reference claims against the retrieved chunks.

complete.why: No advantage over rank metrics here.

holes.why: It does not depend on pre-judged documents, only on judge quality.

blocks.takeaway: Rank metrics are cheap and deterministic but need labels. Judged metrics need no labels but add judge noise. Say which you lack, then pick.

items.symptom: Recall at 10 is 0.92 and answers still miss facts
items.cause: k is larger than the number of chunks the prompt receives
items.fix: Set k to the number of chunks the generator sees, for example 4, and report recall at that k.

items.symptom: A new index scores lower although the results look better
items.cause: New documents have no relevance judgments, so they count as non-relevant
items.fix: Track holes_ratio, judge the new top results and extend the qrels before comparing.

items.symptom: Two libraries report different nDCG for one run
items.fix: Fix one definition in the harness and store it next to the score.

items.symptom: A dense retriever tops a public benchmark and loses on exact identifiers
items.cause: BEIR shows BM25 is a strong baseline, and your queries differ from the benchmark
items.fix: Score on your own queries and keep identifier-heavy cases as their own slice.

items.symptom: Answer relevancy shifts after an embedding change
items.cause: The metric embeds the user input and regenerated questions, so the embedder changes the score
items.fix: Pin the embedding model and the number of generated questions (default 3) in the harness.

items.title: Go deeper: the Foundry Document Retrieval evaluator

blocks.md: `builtin.document_retrieval` is a composite evaluator. It returns Fidelity, NDCG, XDCG, Max Relevance N and Holes, with outputs such as `ndcg@3`, `xdcg@3`, `fidelity`, `top1_relevance`, `top3_max_relevance`, `holes` and `holes_ratio`. Inputs are `retrieval_ground_truth` (a `document_id` plus a `query_relevance_label`) and `retrieved_documents`. Holes count documents that were retrieved without a relevance judgment [[r4]].

items.title: Go deeper: RAGAS API and definitions

blocks.md: PyPI `ragas` was at 0.4.3 (released 2026-01-13) when checked. The docs show the collections API (`ragas.metrics.collections`, with `ascore` and `score`). The legacy `SingleTurnSample` API is deprecated in 0.4 and removed in 1.0. The docs title says Response Relevancy while the class is `AnswerRelevancy` [[r20]].

`ContextPrecision` compares chunks with a reference answer, while `ContextUtilization` uses the generated response instead. Noise sensitivity takes `mode="relevant"` (default) or `mode="irrelevant"` [[r20]].

items.title: Go deeper: what BEIR says about retrievers

blocks.md: BEIR bundles 18 public datasets for zero-shot retrieval. BM25 is a strong baseline. Re-ranking and late-interaction models score best on average but at high compute cost, so a benchmark win is not a latency or cost win [[r42]]. The DeepLearning.AI course on advanced RAG shows the same metrics applied end to end [[r14]].

quiz.q: A retriever is scored on four queries. The first relevant chunk appears at ranks 1, 3, never and 2. What is the MRR? Give the answer to three decimals.
quiz.hint: Reciprocal rank is 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant chunk, and 0 when none is retrieved.
quiz.explain: Reciprocal ranks are 1, 1/3, 0 and 1/2. Their sum is 1.833 and the mean over four queries is 0.458. Treating the missing query as rank infinity gives the 0, and dropping it would wrongly average over three queries and give 0.611.

quiz.q: Which cause best explains these numbers?
options: The embedding model is too small to represent these queries well and needs replacing
The judge is biased toward long answers, so it under-scores the shorter answers it receives
The chunk overlap is too low, so facts are split across neighbouring chunks
k is 10 but the prompt receives 4 chunks, so ranks 5 to 10 never reach the generator
quiz.explain: Recall at 10 counts chunks the generator never sees. Score recall at the k the prompt actually uses. A weak embedder would also lower recall at 10, which here is high. Judge length bias affects answer scoring, not the retrieval number. Low overlap could split facts, but the high recall at 10 shows the relevant chunks were found.

quiz.q: Questions need three chunks combined, and experts graded every chunk from 0 to 3. Which metric is the best primary retrieval score?
options: MRR, because it rewards the earliest correct chunk in every ranked list
Hit rate at 1, because it is the strictest check on the top result
nDCG at k, where k is the number of chunks in the prompt
Precision at 20, because it is the simplest metric to explain to stakeholders
quiz.explain: Graded labels and multi-chunk evidence point to nDCG at the k the prompt uses, because it rewards ranking highly relevant chunks above partial ones. MRR and hit rate at 1 look only at the first correct chunk and ignore the others the answer needs. Precision at 20 is unstable when few chunks are relevant, and it ignores grades and order.

quiz.q: Two libraries report nDCG@4 of 0.985 and 0.993 for the same ranking with relevance 3, 2, 0, 1. Which explanation fits?
options: One uses linear gain and the other uses 2^rel - 1, which weights highly relevant chunks more
One library accidentally leaks the ideal ordering into the predicted ranking, which inflates its score
One of them computes MRR because the labels are graded
Rounding error at the fourth decimal place
quiz.explain: Linear gain gives DCG 4.693 against an ideal 4.762, so 0.985. Exponential gain uses 7, 3, 0 and 1, giving 9.324 against 9.393, so 0.993. The two coincide for binary labels and diverge for graded ones. Leaking the ideal order would give 1.0, MRR is a different metric with a different range, and rounding cannot move the result by 0.008.

takeaways: Pick the retrieval metric by your labels: rank metrics need qrels, judged context metrics do not.
Tie k to the number of chunks the prompt actually receives.
Score retrieval and generation separately. Faithfulness checks support, not truth.
Fix one nDCG definition and track holes_ratio before comparing indexes.
Public retrieval benchmarks say little about your identifiers and paraphrases, so test your own queries.
